Prerequisites: 02 · Matrices and homogeneous transforms, 05 · Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

A camera measures direction on an image plane

A pinhole camera turns a 3D point into an image location using similar triangles. Distance along the camera axis controls apparent size: moving an object twice as far away halves its projected size when its physical size stays fixed. Focal lengths fx and fy are measured in pixels here; cx and cy locate the principal point. Changing image resolution without updating those parameters changes the interpretation.

gffx cameras look down local negative z. Define positive view depth d=-z. With camera x right, y up, and image v downward, the projection is:

Worked example

Take (x,y,z)=(1,0.5,-2), fx=fy=500, cx=320 and cy=240. Depth is two, so the image point is (570,115). If depth doubles while x and y stay fixed, its displacement from the principal point halves. If instead the entire point is scaled from the camera origin, its direction stays fixed and so does its image location.

Depth is essential: one pixel alone defines a ray, not a unique 3D point. View depth is axial distance, not Euclidean range along that ray. NDC depth is another quantity produced by the projection matrix; near and far determine its mapping. Feeding NDC values into an axial-depth formula reconstructs the wrong geometry even when array shapes match.

Validity is not visibility

A finite point behind the camera can still have a mathematically defined perspective divide. gffx preserves that distinction by default and offers in_front_only=True for explicit half-space rejection. Neither mode proves that a point is inside the image, between clipping planes, unoccluded or on a front-facing surface. Masks identify exceptional values; they should not be discarded merely because invalid outputs are finite.

Try the camera playground

A dolly changes camera position; zoom changes focal length; pan rotates the viewing direction from a fixed position. In the studio's dolly-zoom, focal length grows in proportion to the distance from the reference plane z=0. The ratio f/d therefore stays fixed for that plane. If distance changes from 4.5 to 6.5 units, multiply focal length by 6.5/4.5. Background points have a different depth, so their scale changes: that is the illusion. It does not keep every point on a deep bunny fixed.

The external view draws a cyan camera frustum over the scene. These are saved synchronized clips, not a live renderer throughput measurement. In Depth becomes geometry, only covered pixels are unprojected; orbiting the cloud reveals the empty backs. A missing backside is expected from a single depth image.

Try it yourself

Why can a projected landmark fit fail to determine absolute scene scale?

Answer

Scaling both geometry and translation about the camera can preserve projected directions. Extra information such as known dimensions or depth is needed to remove that ambiguity.

Recover the shot

The high-resolution camera demonstration fixes the three-dimensional object and fits seven camera parameters: three orientation angles, three position coordinates and a positive focal scale represented by its logarithm. Ninety-six known mesh landmarks supply the target pixel correspondences. The mean squared reprojection error is minimized with Adam followed by L-BFGS refinement. The outside view shows the actual saved camera poses; the target/result wipe compares rendered images from those poses. Frames are selected real optimizer states, not an invented interpolation toward the answer.

The rendered images explain the consequence of fitting; they are not the objective. This is not recovering an unknown object from a photograph, nor differentiating through a hard visibility boundary. Known geometry fixes the object-scale ambiguity. Convergence on this synthetic fixture does not promise convergence from arbitrary initial poses. The independent derivative curves remain below the presentation.

gffx boundary

The eager Camera object has projection, depth reconstruction, rigs and gradient fixtures. Pose is camera-to-world and grids use pixel centres at column+0.5,row+0.5. Distortion, rolling shutter, calibrated real-data accuracy, export and latency budgets are not established by the pinhole demonstrations. Use the source guide for exact shapes and dtype/device rules.
